hook: In the early 1900s a young chemist at the Guinness brewery in Dublin had a problem. He needed to judge the quality of barley and hops from only a handful of samples, and the statistics of his day assumed you had hundreds. William Sealy Gosset worked out what happens to averages from small samples, published it in 1908 under the pen name “Student”, and gave the world the **t-test**. More than a century later it is still the everyday tool for asking: are these two averages really different?

sections.heading: The problem: comparing averages with small, noisy samples

blocks.p: Plant A’s assembly takes 43 minutes on average, Plant B’s takes 38.5. Training raised test scores from 65.5 to 69. A filling machine averages 497.5 ml against a 500 ml target. Each of these is a difference in means, and each time the question is the same: is the gap bigger than the natural wobble in the data?

The previous chapter tested proportions using the normal distribution. For means there is one extra complication: we do not know the population SD, so we estimate it from the sample. With small samples that estimate is itself shaky, and the t-test is designed to account for exactly that.

blocks.def: A hypothesis test for means. It compares a difference in means with its standard error, and judges the result against the t-distribution rather than the normal, to allow for the SD being estimated from the data.

The observed difference divided by its estimated standard error: how many “noise units” the result is from what H₀ predicts. Values far from 0 (roughly beyond ±2 for moderate samples) are evidence against H₀.

sections.heading: Building the intuition: signal versus noise

blocks.p: Imagine trying to hear a friend in a café. Whether you can make out the words depends on two things: how loudly they speak (the **signal**) and how noisy the café is (the **noise**). A whisper in a library is clear; a shout at a cricket match may be lost.

steps: **The signal is the difference in means.** Plant B is 4.9 minutes faster.
**The noise is the variability**, scaled by sample size: how much the averages would wobble if we re-ran the comparison with different shifts.
**The t-statistic is signal ÷ noise.** A ratio of 3.8 means the difference is almost four times bigger than its typical random wobble.
**More data lowers the noise.** Averaging over more shifts makes the background quieter, so a smaller difference becomes audible.
**Small samples get a stricter judge.** Because the noise estimate itself is uncertain with few observations, the t-distribution demands a bigger ratio before declaring significance.
blocks.title: The café analogy

diagram.caption: With only 5 observations, the t-distribution has fatter tails than the normal, so the cut-off for a two-sided 5% test moves from 1.96 out to 2.776. Small samples must show a bigger signal-to-noise ratio to count as significant.

think.q: Two teams each report a 3-point improvement in average customer satisfaction. Team A surveyed 10 customers, Team B surveyed 1,000. Whose 3 points do you trust more, and why?
think.a: Team B’s. With 1,000 customers the standard error is about ten times smaller (√100 = 10), so the same 3-point signal gives a t-statistic roughly ten times larger. With 10 customers, a 3-point shift could easily be the luck of who answered.

sections.heading: Choosing the right t-test, step by step

children.label: **One-sample t-test**
children.edge: one group vs a fixed target

diagram.caption: Picking a t-test. The key question for two groups is whether each measurement in one group has a natural partner in the other (the same employee, the same machine, the same store).

steps: **State the question as means.** “Is the mean fill volume different from 500 ml?”
**Pick the test** using the tree: one-sample, paired or two-sample.
**Check assumptions:** independent observations; data roughly normal, or a sample large enough for the CLT; no extreme outliers dominating.
**Compute t** = difference ÷ standard error, and its degrees of freedom.
**Get the p-value** from the t-distribution (`scipy.stats.ttest_1samp`, `ttest_rel`, `ttest_ind(..., equal_var=False)`).
**Report** the difference, its 95% CI, the p-value and an effect size.
blocks.title: The procedure

blocks.def: Two measurements that belong together because they come from the same unit: the same employee before and after training, the same car on two fuel blends. Analysing the differences within each pair removes unit-to-unit variation.

blocks.p: **One-sample t-test.** Compare a sample mean with a target value μ₀:

blocks.plain: How many standard errors the sample mean is from the target.
symbols: estimated standard error of the mean

blocks.p: **Paired t-test.** Compute the difference for each pair (after − before) and run a one-sample t-test on those differences against 0. That is all it is.

blocks.plain: Mean of the within-pair differences divided by its standard error.

blocks.p: **Welch two-sample t-test.** For two independent groups, the standard error of the difference combines both groups’ uncertainty. Variances add, so we add the squared standard errors and take the root:

blocks.plain: Difference between the two sample means divided by the standard error of that difference. Welch’s version does not assume the two groups have equal variances, and uses an adjusted (often non-whole) number of degrees of freedom.
symbols: sample variances of the two groups

blocks.callout: Use Welch’s test as your default for two independent groups (`equal_var=False` in scipy). The older “Student” pooled version assumes equal variances; when that is true, Welch loses almost nothing, and when it is false, Welch protects you.

blocks.def: The difference in means divided by a standard deviation of the data (not the standard error). It says how big the effect is in units of natural variation, independently of sample size. Rough guide: 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large.

example.title: One-sample: is the filling machine on target?
example.setup: A beverage plant samples 10 bottles labelled 500 ml: 498, 497, 501, 495, 499, 496, 500, 497, 498, 494. Is the machine’s mean fill different from 500 ml (α = 0.05, two-sided)?
steps: Sum of squared deviations from 497.5 = 42.5, so s = √(42.5 / 9) = 2.173 ml.
t = (497.5 − 500) / 0.687 = −3.64, with 9 degrees of freedom.
Two-sided p-value = 0.0054. The 95% CI for the mean is 497.5 ± 2.262 × 0.687 = 495.9 to 499.1 ml.
example.result: Reject H₀. The machine is underfilling by about 2.5 ml on average, and the whole interval lies below 500. Recalibrate it: underfilling risks regulatory trouble, and the fix is cheap.

diagram.caption: The t-distribution with 9 degrees of freedom. Values beyond ±2.262 are significant at 5%. The observed t = −3.64 sits deep in the left tail; that tail plus its mirror image on the right give p = 0.0054.

example.title: Welch two-sample: does the new plant layout cut cycle time?
example.setup: Assembly cycle times (minutes) on 8 shifts at each plant. Plant A (old layout): 42, 45, 39, 47, 44, 41, 46, 43. Plant B (new layout): 38, 40, 36, 41, 39, 35, 42, 37.
steps: Means: A = 43.375, B = 38.5. Difference = 4.875 minutes.
Sample variances: A = 7.125, B = 6.0.
t = 4.875 / 1.281 = 3.81. Welch degrees of freedom ≈ 13.9.
example.result: Strong evidence that the new layout is faster, by almost 5 minutes per cycle, a very large effect relative to shift-to-shift variation. Caveat: the plants differ in more than layout (staff, products), so this is evidence of a difference between plants, not proof the layout caused it.

example.title: Paired: did the training work?
example.setup: Eight sales staff take a product-knowledge test before and after a training course. Before: 62, 70, 55, 68, 74, 59, 65, 71. After: 66, 73, 57, 73, 77, 64, 67, 75.
steps: Differences (after − before): 4, 3, 2, 5, 3, 5, 2, 4. Mean difference = 28 / 8 = 3.5 points.
SD of the differences = 1.195. SE = 1.195 / √8 = 0.423.
t = 3.5 / 0.423 = 8.28 with 7 degrees of freedom. p = 0.00007.
95% CI for the mean gain: 3.5 ± 2.365 × 0.423 = 2.5 to 4.5 points.
Wrong analysis for comparison: treating the groups as independent (Welch) gives t = 1.06, p = 0.31, “not significant”.
example.result: Every single person improved, and the paired test sees it clearly. The independent test drowns the 3.5-point gain in the much larger differences between people (SDs of about 6.5 points in each group). Using the wrong test would have cancelled a training programme that works.

sections.heading: Assumptions and how to check them

bullets: **Independence.** Each observation (or each pair) must be independent of the others. Ten readings from the same bottle are not ten bottles. This is the assumption that matters most and cannot be fixed by any formula.

**Approximate normality.** The t-test assumes the data (or the paired differences) come from a roughly normal population. With small samples, check a histogram or Q-Q plot. With 30+ per group, the CLT makes the test robust to moderate skew.
**No dominant outliers.** One extreme value can swing both the mean and the SD. Investigate it before testing.
**Equal variances?** Not needed if you use Welch’s test.

blocks.p: When the assumptions fail badly, use a **non-parametric** alternative that works on ranks instead of raw values: the Mann–Whitney U test instead of the two-sample t-test, and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test instead of the paired t-test. They are less sensitive to outliers and skew, at a small cost in power when data really are normal.

right.title: Independent (Welch) t-test
items: Between-unit variation stays in the noise
Needs larger samples for the same power

diagram.caption: Choose by the design of the data, not by which gives the smaller p-value. If the data are paired, an independent test is not “conservative”; it is wrong.

case.title: Guinness and the birth of the t-test
case.story: Gosset’s job at Guinness involved comparing small batches: barley varieties, growing conditions, hop qualities, often with only a few measurements each. Existing methods treated the sample SD as if it were the true SD, which made small experiments look more certain than they were. Gosset derived the correct distribution for a mean standardised by an estimated SD, the t-distribution, and published it in 1908 in the journal Biometrika as “Student”, reportedly because Guinness preferred staff not to publish under their own names. The statistician Ronald Fisher later recognised its importance and built it into the framework of experimental design that farms, factories and laboratories still use.

bullets: **Manufacturing:** one-sample tests that a process mean matches its specification; two-sample tests comparing suppliers or machines.
**Automotive testing:** paired tests of fuel economy or braking distance on the same cars under two conditions.
**A/B testing of continuous metrics:** average order value or session length, usually with Welch’s test and large samples.
**Model evaluation:** paired t-tests (with care) to compare two models’ scores on the same cross-validation folds.
**Independent test on paired data.** As the training example showed, this can hide a strong effect completely.
**Many pairwise t-tests.** Comparing 5 groups two at a time means 10 tests, and false positives multiply. Use ANOVA followed by corrected post-hoc comparisons.
**Tiny skewed samples.** Revenue per customer with 8 observations and one big spender breaks the normality assumption. Use Mann–Whitney or a bootstrap.
**Significance without size.** With 50,000 users per arm, a ₹2 difference in average order value can be significant. Report the CI and judge whether ₹2 matters.
**Correlation is not causation.** A t-test between two plants or two regions shows a difference, not its cause. Only randomised experiments support causal claims.

blocks.callout: A complete t-test report reads like this: “Training raised scores by 3.5 points on average (95% CI 2.5 to 4.5; paired t(7) = 8.28, p < 0.001).” Effect, interval, test, p-value: in that order of importance.

faq.q: What is the difference between a t-test and a z-test?
faq.a: A z-test assumes the population SD is known (or uses proportions with large samples) and compares against the normal distribution. A t-test estimates the SD from the data and uses the t-distribution. For means, the t-test is almost always the right choice; with large samples the two agree.

faq.q: How small a sample can a t-test handle?
faq.a: Technically as few as 2 per group, but power will be very low and the normality assumption cannot be checked. With fewer than about 10 per group, results should be treated as tentative.

faq.q: Should I use Student’s or Welch’s two-sample t-test?
faq.a: Welch’s, by default. It performs nearly as well as Student’s when variances are equal and much better when they are not. In scipy, pass `equal_var=False`.

faq.q: Can I use a t-test on percentages or ratings from 1 to 5?
faq.a: For averages of ratings over many respondents, a t-test is commonly used and usually fine. For yes/no outcomes summarised as percentages, a test for proportions (z-test or chi-square) is more natural.

faq.q: What does “t(7) = 8.28” mean in a report?
faq.a: A t-statistic of 8.28 with 7 degrees of freedom. The degrees of freedom tell the reader which t-distribution was used to compute the p-value.
